project.topic: What if the Moon were made entirely of ice?
project.title: What If the Moon Were Made of Ice?
project.audience: Curious global general audiences age 13+, no science background
project.core_question: If the Moon kept its size and orbit but were made entirely of water ice, what would change for our nights, tides, coasts, wildlife, the deep ocean and the Moon itself?
project.viewer_takeaway: An ice Moon would shine about six times brighter but weigh only a third as much, so the Sun would take over the tides: smaller, clock-regular tides, shrinking mudflats, changed animal nights, possibly weaker deep-ocean mixing, and a Moon slowly turning to vapor, unlike our durable rocky one.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Today's Moon is a rocky body 1,737 km in radius with a mean density of 3,344 kg/m³, orbiting about 384,400 km from Earth and always showing the same face. Its surface reflects only about 12% of sunlight (geometric albedo 0.12), and its dark patches are ancient seas of cooled lava. Its gravity raises most of Earth's ocean tide; the Sun's tide-generating force is about half the Moon's.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: In an instant, the Moon is replaced by a body of exactly the same size, in exactly the same orbit and rotation, made entirely of water ice with only traces of dust. Earth, the Sun and the Moon's distance are unchanged. The film follows what the changed material does: its mass, its brightness, its pull on our oceans and its survival in sunlight.
assumptions: Radius 1,737 km, mean distance 384,400 km, the same month and the same face toward Earth; the swap is gentle and instantaneous, with no impact or debris.

Composition is pure water ice. Pressure inside a Moon-sized ice ball (about 0.4 GPa at the centre) turns the deep interior into denser forms of ice, giving a mean density of roughly 1,000–1,100 kg/m³ (Saturn's nearly pure-ice moon Tethys has 985 kg/m³), so the mass is about 31% of today's (range 28–33%).
The surface is as reflective as Saturn's icy moons (geometric albedo about 0.7–0.8) instead of 0.12.
Tide figures are simple open-ocean (equilibrium) estimates: tide-raising force scales with mass divided by distance cubed. Real coastlines amplify or damp tides in their own ways.

Earth effects are shown for the first years to decades; the ice Moon's evaporation is a geological-timescale process. How such a Moon could form, and its very long-term orbital evolution, are not addressed.
causal_chain: Swapping rock for ice at the same size lowers the mean density from 3,344 to about 1,040 kg/m³, so the Moon keeps only about 31% of its mass.
Fresh ice reflects about six times more sunlight than lunar rock, so the full Moon shines about six times brighter, and with no lava seas the familiar dark 'face' disappears.
Tide-raising force is proportional to mass, so at the same distance the ice Moon raises only about 31% of today's lunar tide, less than the Sun's 46%: the Sun becomes the main tide-maker.
Combined tides shrink to roughly half, and because the solar tide follows the solar day, high tide at each place arrives at nearly the same clock time every day.
Smaller tidal ranges expose less intertidal mudflat, shrinking feeding grounds for migratory shorebirds and changing the rhythm of harbors and fishers.
Brighter moonlit nights shift the behaviour of nocturnal animals: some hide more, while moonlight navigators such as dung beetles could find their way on more nights; fewer faint stars are visible.
Tidal energy scales roughly with tide height squared, so total tidal energy falls to about a quarter; since tides help power deep-ocean mixing, that mixing could weaken, with uncertain consequences.
Sunlit ice turns straight to vapor in a vacuum; some of it escapes each day, so the ice Moon would slowly shrink over the ages, unlike today's rocky Moon.
uncertainties: The ice Moon's exact mass depends on its internal ice phases and temperature; 28–33% of today's mass is a reasonable range, and every tide figure scales with it.
Brightness depends on how space weathering, dust and fresh frost would change the surface over time; 'about six times' is an estimate, not a measurement.
Real tides depend strongly on each basin's shape and resonance; some bays would change by more or less than half, and the timing pattern would carry local delays.
Animal responses to brighter nights vary by species and habitat; the film shows possible behaviour changes, not predicted ecosystem outcomes.
How much weaker tidal mixing would alter deep-ocean circulation, nutrients and climate is genuinely uncertain and is not asserted.
The evaporation rate of an ice Moon is uncertain by roughly an order of magnitude; the vapor itself would be essentially invisible.
Weaker lunar tides would also slow the lengthening of Earth's day and the Moon's outward drift; these slow effects are not shown.

claims.statement: The real Moon has a mean radius of 1,737.4 km, a mean density of 3,344 kg/m³, a mean distance of 384,400 km and a geometric albedo of 0.12.
claims.reasoning: NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet values.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use rounded values; show the rocky Moon with its true dark maria in TODAY shots.

claims.statement: Icy moons are bright and light: Saturn's Tethys, made almost entirely of water ice, has a mean density of 985 kg/m³ and a geometric albedo of 0.8; Rhea (0.7) and Europa (0.68) are similarly reflective.
claims.reasoning: NASA NSSDC Saturnian and Jovian satellite fact sheets.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Mention as the real-world analogue for the ice Moon's surface; do not claim the ice Moon would look exactly like Tethys.

claims.statement: A Moon-sized ball of pure water ice would have a mean density of about 1,000–1,100 kg/m³ and therefore about 31% (28–33%) of the real Moon's mass.
claims.reasoning: Same volume; mass scales with mean density. Central pressure of about 0.4 GPa turns roughly the inner 70% of the radius into denser ice II, giving a mean near 1,040 kg/m³; 1,040 / 3,344 ≈ 0.31.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate 'a third of the mass'; show the cutaway as SCHEMATIC with ice layers simplified.

claims.statement: With an icy-moon albedo of about 0.7–0.8 instead of 0.12, the full ice Moon would appear about six times brighter (roughly 5.7–6.7 times).
claims.reasoning: Full-moon brightness is proportional to geometric albedo at the same size and distance: 0.68–0.8 divided by 0.12.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say 'about six times brighter'; keep camera exposure fixed during the comparison and label the multiplier ESTIMATE.

claims.statement: The Moon's dark patches (maria) are seas of cooled lava that flooded vast impact basins; they make the familiar 'face' patterns. A Moon of pure ice would not have them.
claims.reasoning: NASA describes maria as seas of cooled lava that flooded impact basins between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago; pure ice contains no lava plains.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show the face fading on the ice Moon; do not invent ice-moon surface markings beyond craters and fractures.

claims.statement: Tide-generating force is proportional to a body's mass and inversely to the cube of its distance; the Sun's tide-generating force is about half (46%) of the Moon's.
claims.reasoning: NOAA tides tutorial: tidal forces vary inversely as the cube of distance, and the Sun's tide-generating force is about half the Moon's; 46% follows from the masses and mean distances.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Distinguish tidal force from ordinary gravitational pull in on-screen labels ('TIDAL PULL').

claims.statement: At the same distance, a Moon with 31% of the mass would raise 31% of today's lunar tide, smaller than the Sun's 46%, making the Sun the main tide-maker.
claims.reasoning: Tidal force is linear in mass at fixed distance; 0.31 < 0.46.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show the tidal bulges as an exaggerated, labelled schematic with distances not to scale.

claims.statement: In a simple open-ocean estimate, spring tides would be about 53% and neap tides about 28% of today's, so tides would be roughly half as high overall.
claims.reasoning: Equilibrium tide amplitudes add and subtract: today spring 1 + 0.46 and neap 1 − 0.46; ice Moon spring 0.31 + 0.46 and neap 0.46 − 0.31.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate 'about half as high'; label the tidal-flat comparison ILLUSTRATIVE and note that each coast responds differently.

claims.statement: With the solar tide dominant, high tide at any one place would come at nearly the same clock time every day, wobbling within about ±1.4 hours over two weeks, instead of arriving about 50 minutes later each day as it does now.
claims.reasoning: The solar semidiurnal tide repeats every 12.00 hours; the weaker lunar one (12.42 hours) only shifts the combined peak by up to arcsin(0.31/0.46) ≈ 42° of the 12-hour cycle ≈ 1.4 hours.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Present the tide clock as a schematic; local tides add fixed delays but keep the daily regularity.

claims.statement: Smaller tidal ranges would expose less intertidal mudflat at low tide, shrinking feeding grounds that millions of migratory shorebirds rely on; the Wadden Sea alone, the largest unbroken tidal-flat system, sees an average of 10–12 million birds pass through each year.
claims.reasoning: Exposed intertidal area grows with tidal range; UNESCO describes the Wadden Sea's flats and their 10–12 million passing birds.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say 'would shrink', not 'disappear'; show birds crowding a narrower strip, never harmed.

claims.statement: Moonlight already changes nocturnal animal behaviour: across 58 nocturnal mammal species, prey relying on smell or echolocation were generally less active on bright nights, visual prey more active, and some predators such as lions less active.
claims.reasoning: Prugh and Golden (Journal of Animal Ecology), as reported by the University of Alaska Fairbanks.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use 'some animals would hide'; show retreating eyeshine, not predation.

claims.statement: Dung beetles hold a straight course using polarized moonlight; they manage under a full moon but lose their way under weaker quarter or crescent moons, so a brighter Moon could let them navigate on more nights.
claims.reasoning: Lund University: polarized light from a quarter moon is only one-third as strong as at full moon, and beetles are lost then; six-times brighter moonlight would strengthen the signal at every phase.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Label the sky polarization pattern SCHEMATIC; say 'would navigate better', not 'always'.

claims.statement: About 1 terawatt, 25–30% of all tidal energy dissipation, occurs in the deep ocean over rough seafloor, where it is thought to supply much of the mixing that drives large-scale ocean circulation.
claims.reasoning: NASA Earth Observatory summary of Egbert and Ray (2000), based on TOPEX/Poseidon altimetry.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show the mixing as a labelled cross-section schematic with vertical exaggeration.

claims.statement: Total tidal energy would fall to about a quarter of today's, so deep-ocean mixing could weaken, with consequences for currents and nutrients that cannot be predicted confidently.
claims.reasoning: Tidal energy scales roughly with amplitude squared: (0.31² + 0.46²) / (1² + 0.46²) ≈ 0.25.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate 'could slow'; label 'EFFECTS UNCERTAIN'; no climate-disaster imagery.

claims.statement: On the real Moon, water ice survives only in polar crater shadows that sunlight never reaches, where temperatures never rise above about −250 °F (−157 °C).
claims.reasoning: NASA/JPL announcement of ice confirmed at the Moon's poles.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use as the basis for the evaporation beat; do not show today's Moon losing ice.

claims.statement: Sunlit ice on an ice Moon would slowly turn straight to vapor; much would refreeze on the cold night side, but some would be lost to space, so the Moon would shrink over geological time, far too slowly to notice in a lifetime.
claims.reasoning: Sublimation of exposed ice in sunlight at Earth's distance from the Sun (CL15) plus escape and photodissociation of a fraction of the vapor; the rate is uncertain by about an order of magnitude.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Label the vapor shimmer 'ILLUSTRATIVE · INVISIBLE TO THE EYE'; give no rate or lifetime on screen.

claims.statement: Six-times-brighter moonlight would brighten the night sky on moonlit nights, hiding more faint stars.
claims.reasoning: Moonlight scattered by the atmosphere is the main natural brightener of the night sky; scattered light scales with the Moon's brightness.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show a modest fading of faint stars only, with exposure fixed.

claims.statement: The real Moon has kept its rocky surface for about 4.5 billion years; rock does not evaporate in sunlight the way exposed ice does.
claims.reasoning: The Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago; silicate rock has negligible vapor pressure at lunar dayside temperatures (up to about 390 K).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Closing line only; no numbers on screen.

creative_direction.logline: Our gray Moon frosts into a dazzling ball of ice, and we follow that one change from a moonlit sea to the tides, a shorebird mudflat, a beetle's night journey, the deep ocean and the Moon itself, before the real Moon rises again.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Cool, luminous documentary realism: silver-blue moonlight, glassy blue-white ice, deep navy seas and warm human lights. Schematics are clean, labelled and calm, never cartoonish or apocalyptic.
creative_direction.lighting: Dusk sky light and true-angular-size moonlight over the sea; harsh unfiltered sunlight with deep black shadows in space; dim blue moonlight that brightens about sixfold with exposure locked; soft morning light over the tidal flat; warm practical windows at the harbor.
creative_direction.camera_language: Telephoto moonrise, slow orbit of the Moon in space, straight-on 'face' view, eye-level moonlit jetty, schematic cutaways and tidal bulges, a tide clock, aerial tidal flat, harbor eye level, night meadow and a beetle macro, ocean cross-section push, sunlit-limb orbit, molecular macro, and the same telephoto moonrise to close the loop.
creative_direction.motion_language: Slow, deliberate glides; the changed rule always reads as frost sweeping, light brightening or water staying higher; no restless cutting, one reveal every few seconds.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Earth-surface shots use metres at true scale (person 1.75 m, sailboats 7 m, dung beetle 2.5 cm). The Moon in Earth's sky is always drawn at its true 0.52° angular diameter and enlarged only by telephoto framing. Space shots use 1 unit = 1,000 km with the Moon's true 1.737-unit radius; any compressed Earth–Moon distance, exaggerated tidal bulge or ocean cross-section exaggeration is labelled NOT TO SCALE.
creative_direction.opening_hook: A real gray full Moon rising over a dusk sea frosts over into glittering blue-white ice in a second and a half, and its reflection path on the water flares brighter as the question is asked.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: The ice Moon's sunlit limb breathes faint, labelled vapor; then we return to the dusk sea, where the real dusty gray Moon rises: 'built to last'.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The final frame, the gray Moon rising in the same telephoto framing, is frame 0; the loop restarts as the Moon frosts over again.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse first: Earth globe and NASA textures, starfield, sky dome, ocean surface, terrain, bird flock, humanoid figure, sailboat, grass field, bokeh, snowfall, water molecules, dial gauge, captions, overlay labels, camera rig, film pipeline and audio kit. New components (configurable moon body, tidal flat, tidal bulge diagram, ocean cross-section diagram, dung beetle) are original, parameterised and promoted to the library on this render.

audio.voice_style: Calm, peaceful, warm adult male; intimate documentary voice; natural breathing; wonder without shouting
audio.music_direction: Sparse original score in E minor: a soft glass-harmonica pad and celesta-like bells for the icy reveal, a slow two-swell tidal pulse under the mechanism, warm low strings for coasts and creatures, a held low drone for the deep ocean, a fragile high shimmer for the evaporating Moon, resolving to E major as the gray Moon returns.
audio.sfx_direction: Synthesized and restrained: a crystalline frost crackle as the Moon freezes, gentle surf, distant shorebird calls, harbor water lapping and a rope creak, night insects and a beetle's tiny scuff, a deep muffled ocean rumble, a faint airy hiss for sublimation. No loud impacts or constant whooshes.

captions.style: Premium documentary subtitles: ivory semibold with a thin charcoal outline and soft shadow, restrained amber active word, phrase-by-phrase reveal with a 120 ms ease; a faint navy gradient behind text only over bright moonlit water.
captions.active_word_treatment: The spoken word turns amber without moving the baseline; emphasised phrases keep a soft accent colour, a 1.04 scale or a gentle glow.
captions.highlights_policy: Exact narration only. In-scene labels are limited to TODAY / ICE MOON state chips, SCHEMATIC / ILLUSTRATIVE / NOT TO SCALE tags and approximate numbers backed by the claim register; never more than one highlighted phrase at a time.

narration.text: What if the Moon were made entirely of ice?
narration.delivery_note: Hushed, curious; a small lift on 'entirely of ice'.

scenes.viewer_question: What would an ice Moon look like and do?
scenes.visual_payoff: The familiar gray full Moon frosts over into a blue-white ball of ice and its glade on the sea flares brighter.

shots.world: Open sea at dusk, metres, +Y up, sea level y = 0, looking east. The full Moon stands 1.5° above the horizon at its true 0.52° angular diameter: a sphere of radius 45.4 m centred at [0, 262, -10000]. Calm sea with a low swell; the sun has set behind the camera.

camera.movement: Very slow 40 m push toward the horizon with a slight tilt up onto the Moon.
camera.lens_notes: 3.2° vertical FOV telephoto: the Moon's true 0.52° disc spans about 310 px; compression stacks the moon glade on the water.

subjects.appearance: Starts as today's gray full Moon with dark maria; a frost front sweeps across, leaving a bright blue-white sphere with faint crater rims and fine fractures.
subjects.geometry_and_material: High-segment sphere; rock mode uses a lunar albedo map with maria (geometric albedo 0.12); ice mode uses procedural cracked ice with high albedo (0.75), slight blue subsurface tint and crater normal detail; Lommel–Seeliger lighting; iceAmount blends with a noisy moving front.
subjects.scale_and_accuracy: True angular size (0.52°) and position; enlarged only by the telephoto lens.
subjects.movement: Static in the sky; iceAmount 0 → 1 between 0.6 s and 2.1 s.

subjects.appearance: Dark blue-gray dusk sea with a narrow silver glade under the Moon that widens and brightens as the Moon turns to ice.
subjects.geometry_and_material: Analytic multi-octave wave normals, Fresnel sky reflection and glitter aimed at the Moon direction.
subjects.scale_and_accuracy: Wave height 0.4 m; glade brightness scales with the Moon's albedo (about six times) with exposure fixed.
subjects.movement: Travelling swell from the east; glitter intensity ramps 1.0 → 6.0 between 1.0 s and 2.4 s.

subjects.appearance: Indigo zenith fading to a pale violet horizon band, first faint stars high up.

subjects.scale_and_accuracy: Sun 6° below the horizon behind the camera.
subjects.movement: Static.

animation_plan: 0.0–0.6 s hold on the real gray Moon with its dark maria.
0.6–2.1 s a frost front with crystalline edge sweeps from the upper-left limb to the lower right; maria fade to white; tiny glints sparkle along the front.
1.0–2.4 s the moon glade on the sea widens and brightens about sixfold.
2.2 s state chip 'WHAT IF · MOON OF ICE' fades in top-left.
2.4–4.2 s gentle push continues; swell keeps rolling.
shots.lighting: Dusk sky ambient; moonlight as a directional light from the Moon's direction whose intensity follows the Moon's albedo; camera exposure locked.
effects: Soft bloom on the ice Moon and glade only
shots.composition_notes: Moon centred near y≈620 px, horizon near y≈1060 px, glade leading down toward the captions; chip within the top safe area.

distribution.primary_search_intent: what if the moon was made of ice
core_keywords: what if the moon was ice
distribution.distinctive_angle: Same size, same orbit, but ice: the Moon would shine about six times brighter yet weigh a third as much, so the Sun takes over the tides, high tide keeps nearly the same hour every day, mudflats shrink, wildlife nights change, and the Moon itself slowly turns to vapor.
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Mass, brightness and tide figures are estimates from stated assumptions (density about 1,040 kg/m³, icy-moon albedo, open-ocean tides); effects on wildlife and deep-ocean mixing are presented as possibilities; tidal bulges, the vapor halo and sky polarization are labelled illustrative or schematic. Titles and descriptions must not claim more than the film shows.
